name: THE BRUSSEL AND FLOW BURGER (served with Brussel Sprouts)

recipe.history:
Brussels sprouts, Brassica oleracea var. gemmifera, are a cultivar of the same species that gives us cabbage, kale, broccoli, and cauliflower — a testament to the extraordinary range of food plants that human cultivation has coaxed from a single wild ancestor. Despite their name, Brussels sprouts were not definitively documented in Belgium until the 13th century, though related brassica cultivars were grown in the Mediterranean region centuries earlier. They became a staple crop of the Low Countries — modern Belgium and the Netherlands — where the cool, damp climate proved ideal for their slow, moisture-loving growth. Cultivation spread through northern Europe and eventually to England, where 18th and 19th century kitchen gardens grew them as a reliable winter vegetable. Their reputation in English and American cooking suffered enormously from the habit of boiling them well past any reasonable point of doneness — waterlogged, sulfurous, and gray-green, the boiled Brussels sprout became a symbol of culinary suffering that most people encountered at holiday dinners and avoided ever after. This reputation was almost entirely undeserved, as the vegetable's rehabilitation over the last twenty years has definitively demonstrated.

The Brussels sprout's American culinary resurrection is one of the most dramatic image rehabilitations in the history of American vegetables. Credit is owed primarily to high-heat roasting and the discovery, widespread in restaurant kitchens by the early 2000s, that a sprout roasted or fried until its outer leaves are caramelized and crisp while its interior remains tender and nutty is an entirely different organism from the boiled version. Crispy fried Brussels sprouts became a wildly popular bar snack and appetizer across the country through the 2000s and 2010s, particularly when paired with fish sauce, bacon, lemon aioli, or balsamic reduction. Their arrival on burgers was natural: the same textural and flavor profile that made them great as a bar snack — the crunch, the bitter-sweet caramelization, the earthy nuttiness — translates directly to the burger as a compelling topping that provides substance, interest, and visual drama. Crispy Brussels sprout leaves on a burger function similarly to a great piece of cured meat: they add fat, salt, texture, and depth without taking over.

Brussels sprouts and I were enemies for the first fifteen years of my life because of one specific Thanksgiving at which someone boiled an entire pot of them and served them gray and steaming and I was made to eat several. I did not encounter them again, by choice, until I was in my late twenties and a restaurant I trusted put crispy Brussels sprouts on the table as an amuse-bouche. I ate them with the suspicion of a person who has been lied to, and then I ate all of them and was embarrassed. The caramelization had transformed the glucosinolates — those sulfurous compounds responsible for the sprout's bad reputation — into something roasty, nutty, and sweet. The outer leaves had crisped into something almost like chips. I owe that dish an apology for every unkind thing I thought about Brussels sprouts in the years before it.

Brussels sprouts cooked to their optimal state — roasted hot and fast until caramelized but not dried out — share the same fundamental cooking philosophy as a burger cooked to medium rare. Both are defined by a precise window of done-ness that delivers maximum flavor and texture, and both are irreversibly damaged by overcooking. A medium rare patty at 130 to 135 degrees Fahrenheit is the temperature at which the meat's fat is rendered, its juices retained, and its texture is yielding without being raw. Push past that window and you are making something else, something inferior, and no amount of caramelized Brussels sprouts on top can save it. The lesson of the Brussels sprout — that the method and temperature of cooking are the actual recipe, not just a procedural detail — applies with equal force to every element on the plate. Cook everything correctly, and the burger takes care of itself.
ingredients: For the whole wheat brioche buns:
Kosher salt and cracked black pepper
For the crispy Brussels sprouts topping:
1 lb Brussels sprouts, trimmed, halved lengthwise, and outer leaves separated
4 oz Gruyère or aged white cheddar, sliced
instructions: 1. Make the whole wheat brioche buns: Activate yeast in warm milk with a pinch of sugar, 5–7 minutes until foamy. Combine bread flour, whole wheat flour, honey, and salt in a stand mixer with dough hook.
2. Add yeast mixture and eggs. Mix on low until combined. Increase to medium and add softened butter in pieces. Knead 10–12 minutes until smooth.
3. Cover and refrigerate overnight for cold rise.
4. Next day, divide into 6 portions, shape into tight rounds, and proof at room temperature 2–3 hours until doubled.
5. Preheat oven to 375°F. Brush with egg wash and bake 16–18 minutes until golden brown. Cool on a rack.

6. Roast the Brussels sprouts: Preheat oven to 425°F. Spread halved sprouts and loose outer leaves on a large rimmed baking sheet. Toss with olive oil, salt, pepper, and garlic powder. Roast 20–25 minutes, turning once halfway through, until deeply caramelized and crispy on the edges. In the final 3 minutes, drizzle balsamic vinegar and honey over the sprouts and return to oven to caramelize. Remove and cool slightly.

7. Make the bacon-Dijon aioli: Cook bacon strips in a skillet over medium heat until crispy. Transfer to paper towels to drain. Pour off all but 1 tsp bacon fat and reserve. Once cooled, crumble the bacon finely.
8. Whisk together mayonnaise, whole grain Dijon, regular Dijon, apple cider vinegar, smoked paprika, and salt. Stir in crumbled bacon and reserved bacon fat. Refrigerate until needed.

9. Form patties: Gently combine ground chuck and brisket. Divide into 4 portions (~6 oz each). Form into 3/4-inch thick patties with a thumb indent in the center. Season both sides with kosher salt and black pepper immediately before cooking.

10. Heat a cast-iron skillet over high heat until smoking. Cook patties 3 minutes on the first side. Flip and lay Gruyère slices on each. Cook 2–2.5 minutes more. Pull at 130–132°F and rest loosely foil-tented 3–4 minutes to reach 133–135°F.
11. Toast bun halves in butter until golden.

12. Assemble: Spread bacon-Dijon aioli on both cut faces of each bun. Place radicchio or lettuce on the bottom bun. Set the rested, cheese-topped patty on the lettuce. Pile a generous mound of roasted Brussels sprouts and crispy outer leaves on top of the patty. Close with the top bun. Serve with additional roasted Brussels sprouts on the side.
